newsitem.title: RUSSIA: General sacked by Yeltsin denies any wrongdoing.
newsitem.headline: General sacked by Yeltsin denies any wrongdoing.

text.p: The commander of Russia's land forces, sacked by President Boris Yeltsin for "actions incompatible with his post", said on Monday he was stunned by the news and denied any wrongdoing.

Yeltsin signed an order sacking General Vladimir Semyonov on Saturday "for actions which discredit the honour and dignity of a serviceman and are incompatible with his post", the defence ministry told Reuters on Monday.
But it did not specify what Semyonov, a 56-year-old career officer, had been being accused of.

"This is wholly unexpected," Interfax news agency quoted Semyonov as saying. "I have not received any concrete and convincing accusations from the defence minister and the reasons for my dismissal remain for me unclear."
He said he would fight to clear his name.
Sackings of top officials in Russia are usually phrased vaguely, most often "due to a transfer to another job".
The Russian media have published several articles over alleged corruption in the army top ranks but all those named have denied the allegations.
Semyonov's name has not been mentioned and Interfax quoted military prosecutors as saying he did not figure among several high-ranking officers currently under official investigation.
"We have no materials concerning V. Semyonov that could serve as a reason for his dismissal," Interfax quoted a prosecution office source as saying.
Military experts in the State Duma lower house of parliament told Reuters that Semyonov was personally considered uncorrupt.

But a member of the Duma's defence committee who once served as Semyonov's deputy, Eduard Vorobyov, told Ekho Moskvy radio that the commander shared his ministry's collective responsibility for the sorry state of Russia's once mighty army.
Once the pride of Soviet society, the army has seen morale plummet in recent years amid acute cash shortages and humiliation at the hands of separatists in Chechnya.
Moscow is now pulling its last troops out of the southern region in line with a Yeltsin decree following a peace agreement signed last August that meets many of the rebels' demands.

Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, appointed in July, is battling to instil his authority in the top ranks and to scrape together the extra funds needed to pay servicemen and avert the further disintegration of the forces.

He has played down talk of a military rebellion but has repeatedly warned that the armed forces' problems, including shortages of equipment and supplies, could spin out of control unless spending is increased.
Semyonov will be temporarily replaced as commander of land forces by his deputy, Anatoly Golovnyov, news agencies reported.
Semyonov commanded the land forces of the Soviet Union for a brief period in 1991, until the superpower collapsed in December of that year.
He was appointed chief of the Russian land forces in 1992. In June 1996, Yeltsin promoted him to the rank of army general and several analysts had predicted Semyonov would rise in the ranks.
